For two years I have been actively looking after farm loans in my riding, and I must say that we succeeded last year, by our efforts, in having 15 per cent of the applications-
I repeat, the applications.
-accepted by the Farm Credit Corporation.
And a little further on I said:
This is not to our credit, but I must say this, because I found last year that half the applications for loans were being turned down because of political partisanship.
Those are the words I uttered and the reply of the Minister of Agriculture may be found at the bottom of the same page:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order, 1 should like to give the committee some details concerning the hon. member's riding. Out of 1,500 projects he said that barely 100 were accepted. The corporation reports that for the four constituencies in the lake St. John district there were a total of 369 persons who contacted the local credit adviser for loans during the fiscal year. The dominion bureau of statistics figures for the census of 1961...

I ask
leave under standing order No. 26 to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent national importance, namely the right of the Prime Minister, without any legal authority, to display an unauthorized flag on the property of the crown, stating that this is being done at the request of certain members of parliament.
I submit that this matter is of great importance, and the urgency of debate is substantiated by the fact that the right hon. gentleman intends to take this unprecedented action, within a few hours of which he informed the house yesterday. As a matter of fact the flagpole has already been erected on the grounds in front of this building-

speechtext:
This is an attempt to influence the public of Canada by flying on government property, here on the grounds of parliament, a flag which is the personal choice of the Prime Minister and not the choice of the people of Canada.
It is a rare thing, Mr. Speaker, for a motion to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance to be allowed, because so frequently it is possible to suggest there will be other opportunities to debate the matter, that the matter has not been raised early enough, and arguments of that nature. Beauchesne, in his fourth edition at page 90, citation 100, paragraph 3 says:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
This motion comes within that citation because the opportunity for debating the proposed action will lapse just within a few hours. The Prime Minister told us yesterday that his personal choice will be flown from the flagpole at five o'clock today. It is now about 11.30, and if the house is to pass judgment on this unusual action it must imme-
Display of Canadian Flag diately have a chance to debate the purpose of the Prime Minister's action.
Beauchesne refers to the fact that public interest must demand that discussion take place immediately. If this opportunity were postponed it would be too late. Consequently we are suggesting that under the rule of urgency of debate, this motion is in order. I think, sir, that on a reference to Erskine May's sixteenth edition you will find also that this particular motion meets any of the objections which are sometimes raised when such motions are brought before the house. May points out that the matter must be definite and must deal with a single, specific matter. This motion deals with a single, specific matter, the determination of the government to fly an unauthorized flag-

Therefore it is obvious that other designs may be desired by other members.

The issue here is not the flag but, as I said in the motion, the legality of displaying this flag on government property. The point is not to debate the flag issue but the principle involved, which is the right of the Prime Minister of Canada to circumvent and ignore order in council No. 5888 assented to on September 5, 1945. The argument is not what flag is flown; there is a principle at stake here. What right has the Prime Minister to circumvent a statute or an order in council? I think all these other remarks which have been made miss the point, and I still come back to my argument that this parliament should have the right to say whether anyone has the right to circumvent or ignore one of the statutes of Canada.

It seems to me that there is little doubt about the urgency of this matter because there is a deadline this afternoon, and we must decide whether the proposed flag will or will not be flown. So under the heading of urgency, the matter does seem to be urgent. It also seems to me that the matter is national in scope, particularly in view of the great interest shown by all Canadians on the subject. However, it is my duty to point out to hon. members that under standing order 26 the words are:
Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance-
The standing order provides that a motion be made for the adjournment of the house, which means that discussion could range all day if necessary, and at the end of the sitting time no conclusion would have been reached and no decision would have been made. But we would have had an all day discussion on the subject matter.

Instead of losing the whole day discussing this matter, which is of great emotional import, I would have hoped that the discussion this morning would have given a certain amount of satisfaction to hon. members, and I doubt whether much more can be said on the question after the brief debate which has just taken place. I ask myself whether there is now any real urgency for debate, after having had a small, miniature debate already this morning. Therefore in the circumstances I do not see that urgency, that necessity to set aside the important business already on the order paper in order

to continue the small pocket debate we have already had this morning.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
I wonder if I may direct an extremely important question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, one which I am glad has not


been pushed to one side by the silliness of the motion we have just dealt with. Could I ask the minister whether he has any up to date information about what I understand to be an extremely disastrous flood situation in British Columbia.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SITUATION
speechtext:
I indicated some days ago that there were worrisome days ahead for British Columbia due to the extremely late run-off and the considerable increase in temperature. I will admit at once that the next several days are going to be extremely difficult for the people in the valleys.
The Mission gauge stood yesterday morning at 22.07 feet. This is a height which gives ground for anxiety. At Hope the flow is 420,000 feet per second; at Prince George the gauge stands at 32.07 feet and the water level will rise over the next several days, as is anticipated also at Hope and Mission. Nevertheless there has been no serious breaching of any dikes, although there has been loss and damage, both in the private and the public sectors, as a result of seepage through the dikes and underneath the dikes. I will say at once that this loss is, in total, not inconsiderable. On the Skeena the gauge stood this morning at 38.6 feet. The second crest is about to occur and it is likely to be of the nature of the first. Considerable flooding has taken place in that area. The Peace river, too, is experiencing a flow unprecedented in history. It is now running at 275,000 feet per second and this is causing a great deal of concern, especially with regard to the construction work which is being carried on, because I believe the diversion tunnels are designed to deal with a capacity involving 300,000 feet per second.
I can only say we are hopeful that no critical dikes will be breached, and if we can get over the next week we shall be safe for at least another 12 months.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SITUATION
speechtext: A supplementary question. Could I ask the minister whether he or the government has received any request or communication from the government of British Columbia in relation to federal assistance in overcoming these difficulties; and if not, has the government of Canada made an offer to work with the provincial government so as to minimize the damage caused?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SITUATION

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for giving me an opportunity to pursue my question of privilege at the opening of this sitting.
I was saying that I had some reason to believe that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) had-perhaps inadvertently-misinformed the house last night when answering some arguments of mine. I read over this morning those arguments and that statement of the minister, which I found on page 4218 of Hansard, where he put words in my mouth
Farm Credit Act
to the effect that out of 1,500 requests, only about a hundred were accepted. I never mentioned those figures; I simply stated that 15 per cent of the loans had been accepted in my county.
In order to rectify the fact, Mr. Chairman, I telephoned this morning to the Roberval office of the Farm Credit Corporation and spoke to the official now responsible for that agency, with some witnesses on the line, so that it could not be alleged that I was making up those figures, as it was suggested last night. I gave this telephone call to the new incumbent because, last night, I somewhat put the blame on the credit advisers, but I shall tell you in two minutes that I found out something new.
The minister's words last night somewhat enlightened me and made me discover another reason which prevents the Quebec farmers from obtaining the farm loans to which they are entitled. I called up the new incumbent, because I have the pleasure to announce that the Minister of Agriculture replaced the former adviser for the county of Roberval. So, I called that office where I received some information.
Now, note this. The minister stated that 369 requests had been filed in our four counties and 121 loans had been granted, but I maintained there had been a much greater number of requests. I maintain that today, and I have proof, which I hold from the head of the Roberval office, who told me that, at the first stage of applications-and that is precisely the point to which I want to call the minister's attention, for I believe he has been misled by the Quebec report- first of all, requests are received, and the head of the office tells me that at that stage applications are not registered-and I make a distinction between applications and registered applications-about 30 per cent of farmers' applications are rejected. So, when I said the number of our farmers' applications was much larger than 369, it was because I considered that those received at the office were applications for loans.
Mr. Chairman, it is precisely at the second stage that all sorts of contradictory actions are taken, that 30 to 35 per cent of loan applications made by farmers are refused, and then the whole question is re-examined. It is at the second stage that they say that there were 369 applications, that is farmers have been allowed to make application to the Farm Credit Corporation by depositing $10. I believe that the minister has in his possession information concerning the second

Farm Credit Act
stage only, that he has never been provided with information concerning the first stage.
Taking into consideration that a minimum of 30 per cent of the applications are refused, it is easy to establish the percentage, even at the second stage, of farmers who are denied loans. Considering that the minister stated that 121 applications had been accepted, I have reason to say that in the four ridings (because we have a district office for the four ridings) hardly 15 per cent of the farmers were allowed a farm loan.
I said also that, after having studied the question for approximately a year and a half, I had finally come to the conclusion that this situation was probably due to credit advisers who did not perform their duties adequately.
As can be seen on page 4219 of Hansard, the minister stated:
The dominion bureau of statistics figures for the 1961 census indicate that there were 1,244 farmers in the municipality of Lake St. John West who had gross sales of over $1,200. During the fiscal year ended March 31, 1964, the corporation approved 121 loans for an amount of $1,293,900 in this county, or about one loan for every ten farmers with a gross income of $1,200 or more.
Mr. Chairman, that is precisely the secret I have been trying to find out for a long time and the statement made by the minister provided the answer. He mentioned applications approved at the second stage.
I was wondering why between 35 and 40 per cent of applications for loans from farmers were rejected at the first stage. Now, I know it is because it was discovered that their gross income was less than $1,200. The minister told us last night that the corporation makes loans only to farmers who can prove that their income is above $1,200. This means that loans are granted to farmers whose gross income is $5,000, $6,000, $8,000 and $10,000, but that no money is loaned to the farmer whose income is less than $1,200. In other words, loans are granted to the rich, but they are denied to those who need them. That is how I see it.
Mr. Chairman, even if the minister misinterpreted my remarks last night, he nevertheless gave us an explanation; he gave us evidence, once more, that the government encourages those who have money and discourages those who have none.
That is exactly why we fight and want those loans to be granted to farmers who do not earn more than $1,200 and who own two, three and even four lots, but are refused a loan of $6,000, $7,000 and $8,000 which would enable them to live advantageously and develop their lots.

On several occasions, I called on the adviser and he told me that the act did not allow it. It is understood that, in my area, the act does not authorize loans to the small farmer; the farmer has to be rich to borrow. On account of conditions prevailing in the province of Quebec, it is therefore useless to speak about improving our land, since 60 per cent of our farmers earn less than $1,200 per annum.
The minister keeps making comparisons with the province of Saskatchewan, and says -please note this because it is good:
The hon. member related loans in his constituency to the number of loans being made in the province of Saskatchewan. The d.b.s. figures show that, in 1961, there were 82,285 farmers in Saskatchewan with gross income of over $1,200.
In Saskatchewan, 82,285 farmers earn more than $1,200 per annum. Now, more loans are made to farmers in Saskatchewan precisely because those farmers are richer than those in the province of Quebec.
And the minister adds:
During the last fiscal year, the corporation approved 2,332 loans in Saskatchewan, or about one loan for every 40 farmers.
Mr. Chairman, if the minister wishes to make comparisons, he should go back a few years. He said 121 loans were granted in my constituency, but I should like to know the total number of loans granted in the province of Quebec in 1964.
Then the minister goes on:
From this it will be seen that the rate of lending by the corporation in the hon. member's constituency is about four times as high as in the province of Saskatchewan-
This is untrue. I am not very good at mathematics, in fact, some are better than I am, but while in 1962, 109 loans were granted in the province of Quebec, 1936 were granted in Saskatchewan. The minister would have us believe that 109 is higher than 1936.
In 1963, the province of Quebec succeeded in obtaining 104 loans against 2,307 in Saskatchewan. Will the minister again try to make us believe that 104 is more than 2,307.
In 1964, in Saskatchewan, 2,300 loans were granted. The minister will likely say that there are more people there; he will try to make comparisons between the population and the number of farmers. But I am prepared to put my seat at stake if the province of Saskatchewan has a greater population than the province of Quebec.
We are told that four times as many loans are granted in the province of Quebec than

in the province of Saskatchewan. How ridiculous can one be. You have put your finger on the trouble: namely that 2,307 loans were granted in Saskatchewan to farmers who are well off, while in the province of Quebec where our farmers really need loans, only a very small number were made.
The province of Quebec should be getting 5,000 loans a year, against 300 for Saskatchewan. That would be a fair proportion considering the taxpayers. Just figure it out: the province of Quebec pays five times more taxes than Saskatchewan. I have nothing against Saskatchewan, but I maintain that the province of Quebec is entitled to the same fair treatment.
If the Minister of Agriculture wants to study the situation and be responsible, let him compare the number of small farmers, not the rich farmers but the poor ones, in Quebec and in Saskatchewan. Then the figures could be reversed and doubled, and 5,000 loans would have to be granted in Quebec and only 300 in Saskatchewan, so that those two provinces could be given the same treatment.
That is the core of our agricultural problem. The needs of the province of Quebec where family farms have to be improved have never been understood. The minister's statements concerning family farms indicate that he has never known such farms nor considered their proportions.
In the application of the law as it stands at present, no consideration can be given to farmers who earn less than $1,200 a year. That is precisely what we have been criticizing for the past four or five years. As I said last night, when a farmer goes to the office, the credit adviser tells him without too much explanation: "Sell your farm and move to the city."
Only last night I got another letter from a farmer who owes $5,000 on his two farms, and yet he has 155 acres under cultivation. All he needs is a small $2,000 loan to complete his organization. But he is told to sell his farms and to leave.
What a fine reasoning. People are being paid to advise and help farmers, but this is not the way to revive agriculture in the province of Quebec, and more especially our family farms.
We were justified in the past to ask for a minister of agriculture for the province of Quebec and we shall keep on making such a demand, because I realize more and more that the legislation implemented by the min20220-269
Farm Credit Act
ister in the western provinces is not adaptable to the province of Quebec.

I will come back to the subject under discussion; this was only an aside to illustrate how amendments to the Farm Credit Act even though they offer a few benefits, are still favouring western and not eastern Canada, and that is because the problems of the eastern farmers were never seriously considered.
The introduction of these new credit terms is intended to make our farmers agricultural contractors, as in western Canada. These family farms which were handed down from generation to generation are going to disappear. It is for that reason that we want to safeguard the soil of Quebec, because we must protect our family life in all spheres of society.
I consider that if the proposed amendments were more appropriate to the kind of farming carried out in Quebec, our farmers would be able, a few years hence, to compete on an equal footing with those farmers of other provinces. Our farmers merely ask for the same standard of living as that of other provinces. But what is being done today? They are shown to the door and told to go into town and to leave their farms.
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased with these amendments because two or three of them have to do especially with beekeeping and other types of farming. Farm production, in the province of Quebec, is so highly diversified that instead of these amendments, we should have had at least 10 or 12 more directly related to Quebec farming. I am sure we will get nowhere as long as the Minister of Agriculture does not examine the question. I know he can do it if he wants to. Let him come to Quebec not as someone dealing occasionally with people but as one who considers the type of farms we have and the living conditions of our farmers and, Mr. Chairman, I can guarantee that we will have only words of praise for him in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I listened to the hon. member for Roberval I could not help but think that if the Creditiste party in this house stuck with the issues about which

Farm Credit Act
he spoke today instead of following will-o'-the-wisp issues such as the flag, which means nothing to the people of rural Quebec, and helped the people in his county by joining with us in trying to get some long range program to help the smaller farmer across the country, we would be in a much better position than we are today with regard to agriculture.
I rise to speak on the amendments to the Farm Credit Act. Some two or three weeks ago I indicated to the Minister of Agriculture that we on this side of the house would welcome legislation brought in that was positive, constructive and would do some good for at least some section of the Canadian people. Therefore I was pleased when the Farm Credit Act amendments were brought down. However, in reading over the debate, and particularly the minister's words yesterday, I was shocked to find that what I thought was just poor drafting in the bill is a deliberate policy on the part of the government.
I am referring to the cost of money. We had a farm loan board in existence in Canada from 1929, and until 1957 all the farm loan board was able to lend was approximately $110 million. This works out to roughly $4 million or $5 million a year. The reason they could not fill this big demand that arose as the result of a revolution in agriculture was the attitude of those who administered the farm loan board. This board was under the Department of Finance, and their concept of a loan was "If you want $5,000, show us $10,000 worth of assets and then we will give you a $5,000 loan".
The revolutionary, new concept that was brought in in 1959 with the Farm Credit Corporation was altogether different. This new concept was that we were trying to help agriculture to get on its feet so that more and more farmers could become commercial in their operations. I wish the hon. member for Roberval would not keep referring to these "rich" farmers in Saskatchewan. What he is really trying to say is that compared with the people in his county, many people in other parts of Canada are commercial farmers and are farming to make money. It is just as true to say this, because the wealthiest farmers in Canada are actually in the province of Ontario, where in proportion they number twice as many as there are in Saskatchewan. The job of this government and our job as representatives in this parliament is to help more and more farmers reach the commercial level of farming; and the Farm

Credit Act was one of the best acts ever put on the statute books of this country to help that development. Now the very philosophy of that act is being attacked; its basic, fundamental purpose is being changed. The basic, fundamental purpose of the act was to stabilize the cost of money to the agricultural industry in order to assist those who wanted to go into commercial farming.
If you look at the history of debt in Canada -that is, debt held by the federal government -you will find, when you apply the amount of interest paid to the total amount of debt, that the average interest rate fluctuates between 3 per cent and 4 per cent. It is true that during temporary periods of around four, five and six years the interest rate goes above 4 per cent, and there are other periods when it goes below 3 per cent; but the average amount paid by the treasury of Canada to the people of Canada who lend money to the government varies, on the total debt, between 3 per cent and 4 per cent. I am not talking about the day by day cost of money; I am simply talking of the average interest paid on the total debt.
We had this issue before us when we formed the government, and we decided that if we were to bring the agricultural industry up to a higher level so that it could participate in the wealth of this country we had to give to the industry some assurance that if a farmer borrowed money for 30 years there would be a stabilized interest rate, and we picked 4 per cent as the basic interest rate that we would charge farmers.
We added to it 1 per cent to cover the costs of running the corporation and to provide a reserve against loss. We took the maximum of the average interest rate paid by the government of Canada to the people of Canada for borrowing money-because the long term average on the total debt is, as I said, 3 per cent or 4 per cent-and we were going to ask the farmers, in periods of low interest rates when the government was getting the money at below the average interest rate, to continue to pay 5 per cent so we would build up a reserve when the country swung into a high interest period, and this reserve would carry the Farm Credit Corporation through without the government having to come back to this house and ask for money. We were prepared as a government, if that reserve did not build up and the Department of Finance took the loss, to say to the farmers that they had not a fluctuating interest rate but a stable interest rate.

Therefore the issue was very simple. On the question of the basic principle of providing farm credit to lift more and more farmers to the commercial level we decided to take a stabilized rate of 4 per cent plus 1 per cent to cover costs, so that when the interest rate was low the farmer would pay 5 per cent and when the interest rate was high he would still only pay 5 per cent. We took the highest level so that in the long run there would be no cost to the treasury, and no subsidization.
The government has now changed the principle drastically. I did not realize how drastic was the change until I read the remarks made by the minister last night, as reported at page 4216 of Hansard. I would ask every hon. member in this committee, whether he comes from a rural constituency or an urban constituency, to write these figures down and calculate them, and then go back to his voters and ask for their support for this sort of thing. This is what the minister said:
If a farmer were to borrow $40,000, his payment on the first $20,000 would be $1,322 a year-
I ask hon. members to put those figures down and to work them out. What does it come to at $1,322 a year? It works out to a rate of 6.6 per cent on the first $20,000. The minister went on:
-and his payment on the other $20,000 would be $1,551-
That works out to 7.7 per cent. Then the minister went on to say:
-so his gross payment plus taxes

-and I do not know how taxes got into this-
-would be $2,873.
That works out to an average of 7.2 per cent over the whole loan. When I read those remarks, Mr. Chairman, and when I read over the previous debate during which the minister and the hon. member for Essex South were lamenting about farmers having to go out and pay 10 per cent for money borrowed if they wanted more than the maximum of $20,000 and $27,500, it seemed a terrible thing. The hon. member for Essex South referred to these people who lend money as Shylocks. The more polite term for them is "loan sharks". But who is the loan shark now?

I hear a voice saying I am wrong. I can only go by what the minister says and by what is contained in the amendment before me. If what the minister said earlier about the manner in which these rates are to be charged was correct, then the interest rates I have quoted are also correct. If I am wrong I want to find out. We do not wish to hold up good legislation, and this is good legislation. I know that every year or so it has to be amended, and we intend to support these amendments. But these doubts have been placed in our minds after reading what the minister said earlier in this debate and after reading the amendment. It may be that the minister intends to change the cost of money on the upper part of the loan far beyond the additional penalty which has been mentioned, and to carry that cost right down to the whole amount.

I know how the minister feels about amendments to this act. This legislation is intended to help certain types of farmers, the farmers who are trying to establish commercial farms. It is not supposed to help a man farming in a really big way. But these provisions certainly cannot help those with low incomes, as those the hon. member for Roberval has talked about. Neither, by and large, can it help young people to become established and this, above everything else, is one of the things I should like to see accomplished by this legislation; because young people today cannot be assisted unless they have a father or some other relative who is able to help them. Eventually, I hope, many of these young people can be raised to the status of commercial farmers.
When I was minister I had this problem before me and I had one or two ideas about it; I had been hoping that in these amendments a start, at least, would be made. I had hoped to bring them forward in 1962 when I brought in some amendments, but a doubt remained as to whether the ideas we had at that time would have worked in practice. The provinces of Ontario and Manitoba both felt there were weaknesses in the act in this respect. They themselves brought in bills to help young farmers.
I hope the minister's advisers will continue to work on this problem of young farmers so that we may be presented with amendments likely to be of assistance to them. I know that the precedents in the United States are not altogether suitable for us in Canada, but I do think a move in this direction is the big task before us.
I will close by expressing the hope that when we get to the particular clause concerned the whole question of interest rates will be cleared up, with examples, so that we know what interest rate can be expected in connection with loans of the type under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, as almost everybody says, I did not intend to speak on this matter at all. However, I find I am constrained to speak because of certain remarks the minister made last night. The minister must be corrected because should such remarks go forth from here unchallenged he will be in worse odour in the farming regions than he is now. First of all, the minister said about the farmers last night, as found on page 4222 of Hansard:
Some of them may even need money to finish putting in their crops.
It takes about three months for inspection and appraisal of the land to be made, and if a farmer made an application now he would be pretty late getting his crop in by the time he got any money from the Farm Credit Corporation. He would certainly have to wait a long time.
The remarks that the minister made about lawyers do not have very much to do with the bill but nevertheless they were made in discussing it. When the minister makes remarks in this regard such as he did, I think he cannot know what is going on in his department. Lawyers are not too plentiful in my part of the country, and in my constituency there are five. There are two firms in the town of Vegreville. One firm is headed by my Liberal predecessor in the house. That firm was doing some of the work. The junior partner in the other firm is the Liberal heir apparent in my constituency. Both these firms were doing this work.
The processing of Farm Credit Corporation loans was taken away entirely from the firm headed by the former Liberal member of parliament for my constituency and all the work in the constituency of Vegreville was given to the other firm. Believe it or not, work was taken away from the senior partner in that firm and given to the junior partner. The same girl will do the work and the only difference will be that a different man in the same firm will sign the documents. Believe me, that is a smart way of doing business. Incidentally, both these men were at one time

very strong Liberals. As a matter of fact, the lawyer from whom the work was taken away was the returning officer in my constituency for 30 years. I do not think the minister knows what is going on in this regard.
I might say that I was told by a senior official of the Farm Credit Corporation that the processing of loans by the lawyer who had been the returning officer for that constituency was done more quickly than by any other lawyer in the province of Alberta. But the work was taken away from him and transferred across the hall to another lawyer in the same firm. The same girl will be looking after the work, so there is not a hope in hades of the work being done any more quickly or efficiently. However, that is by the way. I just wanted to put that on record.
The minister is very worried about farmers moving away from the farms, and he may well be. While Bill No. C-100 no doubt is a very good bill and the amendments will work quite nicely for farmers who have two or three sections of land, the bill makes no provision whatever for people with only a quarter section. A quarter section can be an efficient, economic unit. People can make a living from a quarter section if they want to work hard enough. I am talking about the west. I do not know what conditions are in Quebec or Ontario. But the Farm Credit Corporation is under the impression that the smallest amount of land that can constitute an economic unit is half a section. That is the premise on which they work.
Now, if a man has a quarter section and he needs, say $5,000 in order to get another tractor-no, I had better not say a tractor, because then he could get a farm improvement loan-but let us assume he requires something else, then he cannot get any help from the Farm Credit Corporation because there is no provision for it. I found the same fault with this act when it was first brought into being. It provides for a large outlay, but does not go down the scale far enough to provide for smaller amounts. If one is thinking in terms of two quarter sections of land in Alberta, stock and equipment to operate it properly, then that takes quite a little bit of money, especially if the farm is purchased as a going concern.
However, let us assume a man wants a loan of $5,000 to help straighten out his business. What happens? The Farm Credit Corporation inspector comes out and says "You will have to have another quarter section; perhaps you can buy an adjoining piece of land and that will cost you about $10,000 if you

are lucky". Then, the stock tor that quarter section will cost another $5,000 or $6,000, so in order to get a loan of $5,000 this man will have to go into debt to the extent of about $16,000 more to the Farm Credit Corporation because they want him to have an economic unit. This is not where assistance to the farmers should start. Assistance to the farmer should start at the bottom, where the need is greatest. It is the farmers who are on small, family farms who need assistance, these people with a quarter section. They do not want to extend their operations because, perhaps, they are getting on in years and may not have any family. I mean they are not likely to be 20 years old, and they have no family to whom to turn over the farm. They just want to get the farm organized so it can be worked efficiently by the man himself.
People of this type cannot get any help, so I think provision should be made in this bill to cover such situations. The object of the bill is very good. It is to increase the capital available to be lent to the farmers of Canada, and that is very good. But when it comes to increasing the size of the loan up to $55,000, then I say one would need to have a big operation to make this economically feasible. I do not believe a farm could carry a loan of that size unless it consisted of at least two and a half sections or about 1,600 acres. The idea seems to be that the farmer is expected to borrow himself rich. This is something that cannot be done. I feel that in the majority of cases $55,000 is too large an amount to be made available, especially if the interest on the amount over $20,000 is going to be set at 6J per cent or 7 per cent. The payment of interest on a loan of that size will just about take all the profit a man will be able to make from his farm in a year.
I say to the minister therefore that he should draft his amendments so they will include the small farmer, the farmer with a quarter section. He should make the 5 per cent interest rate mandatory, whatever the size of the loan that is granted. A 6J per cent interest rate is too great a strain on any business such as a farm. I say to the minister that the more $55,000 loans that are made and the more interest the farmers have to pay, then the more farmers we will find moving off the land. The farmers who move off the land are mostly those who have small farms and who just cannot get help. They cannot compete under the conditions with which they are faced. I believe these amend-
Farm Credit Act
ments would be a lot better if they included help for the people on a quarter section.
As I said that my remarks were going to be brief, I think I will make any further remarks I have to make on the other clauses of the bill as they come before the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have a few more questions to ask before we pass the first clause. I am not yet convinced on this question of the credit corporation making large loans. I am somewhat concerned that the amendments increasing the size of the loans to $40,000 or $55,000 might cause an undue increase in the cost of land. I should like the minister to give me some idea as to what relationship there is between the price of the land and the loan. I suggest in some cases in western Canada it is perhaps 50 per cent of the going price of the land. If I am wrong in this suggestion, I should like the minister to correct me. This has been my experience in some areas in which the Farm Credit Corporation has operated.
If my assumption is correct, then I believe that an applicant for a $40,000 loan would be buying an $80,000 farm or between $80,000 and $100,000. This leads one to ask where the prospective purchaser would get the other $40,000 or $50,000 which would be needed, after borrowing $55,000 under part III of this act. I come back to my conclusion that these provision are a direct help to the large farmer who has the extra $50,000 in his pocket and who goes to the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow another $40,000 or $50,000.
I should like to correct any false impression the minister may have in his mind when he suggested yesterday that I had a great deal of land in the Hanna district. The Hanna district lies east of Calgary some 200 miles from the Rocky mountains. It has been referred to on many occasions as the dried out part of Alberta. During the thirties farmers were shipped out from that area and the government paid the cost of shipping them out. Much of this area was broken up at one time, but now has been allowed to go back to grass. It is an area which, to some extent, is a bit behind the rest of the province of Alberta. If anyone has not got a large holding of land he cannot survive in that area because it takes 50 acres to support one cow. I do not know whether the minister was fully aware of this, and that most people in the Hanna area have to have a fairly large provincial lease in order to run a fair amount of cattle. I mention this so that it may receive better understanding.

Farm Credit Act
I am pleased with the corporation's operations in this district which is a unique one in its own regard. It does not operate in the municipality. It operates under what the Alberta government calls special areas. They will only allow one cow to 50 acres, and you cannot buy the land from the provincial government. There are something like 3 million acres under provincial lease, and in 1961, or the spring of 1962, the federal government and the Farm Credit Corporation worked out an agreement with the province whereby money could be lent on this leased land for the purchase of it.
That was a major step forward in this dried out part of Alberta. It is an area which suffered tremendous economic losses during the thirties, recovered to some extent during the forties, but is still at the far end of what might be called an agrarian revolution with regard to enlarging farms. In order to enlarge their holdings most farmers in this area must have an opportunity to buy out their neighbours. In fact, any person coming into a special area cannot purchase land until it has been advertised for one month and the local residents have an opportunity to meet the price which the outside purchaser is prepared to offer. If a local resident meets this price, then he gets the land and the outside person has to go somewhere else to look for a place. The reason the provincial government has written this provision into its special areas act is to try and help local farmers enlarge their holdings.
In many cases when leased land comes up for sale all a resident farmer needs is a small loan, something in the neighbourhood of $10,000 to $15,000 to enlarge his holding. As I say, this is a unique area in Canada but it is an area in which the corporation, during the short term of years it has been operating there, has played a great part. I hope it will continue to play an even greater part.
I have mentioned that the district went through a tremendous economic upheaval in the thirties, with the result that bankers, lending institutions, and more particularly the old farm loan board would not venture into the area to make loans. Now the corporation is doing a tremendous job of work in the district and out of one office in Hanna it lent something like $500,000 last year. This is a small amount compared with the totals loaned in other parts of Alberta and throughout the country, but it helped a great many farmers in the district.
Under the new scale of loans proposed in this bill $500,000 would represent only 10

loans. There are some 3,000 farmers still operating in this district and I would like to see more than 10 of them benefit from loans given by the corporation.
There is a tremendous lot of cultivated land in many parts of my constituency, and in these areas it has been my experience that the corporation lends something in the neighbourhood of half the going price. If this is not the case I would like the minister to correct me, but if it is, it suggests that a purchaser must have another $30,000 to $50,000 to back up his proposed loan in order to buy a farm, and if he has this he does not need a loan from the corporation.
Last night the minister told the committee what he thought an economic unit should be. He said that a dairy farmer must have a big enough milk contract to justify his operation and provide his family with a good standard of living. He suggested that a dairy farmer should have 100 acres of pasture for his cattle, and that an economic beef herd in eastern Canada should include 50 cows. I would like to think that the same would apply to western Canada and, if I am wrong, again I invite the minister to correct me.
Further, before we pass clause 1, I would ask the minister to enlarge upon what he feels is too large a unit upon which the corporation should make a loan. We are all aware of the principle upon which the corporation was set up, that of helping those who need help most. Last night the minister said there were still many farmers who operated too large holdings to receive loans under the Farm Credit Corporation. He has outlined what he considers a minimum holding should be, and I would like him to outline what he considers is the maximum holding. He may point his finger at me, meaning I qualify under the minimum. I am pleased to hear that.
My neighbours and I have suffered severe drought conditions during the past three or four years, but we have been able to survive this by shipping in feed, by a tremendous expansion of P.F.R.A., and by pumping water into dugouts. We have gritted our teeth and borne with the dry weather of the past few years. This year we hope that once again we will be able to grow some feed of our own and raise some crops. This is considered the poor area of Alberta. Sometimes I have referred to it as the forgotten part of Alberta, and certainly from time to time the Alberta government has completely forgotten about it.

I would like the minister to outline what the corporation considers a maximum unit for a dairy herd, a beef herd and a grain farm. Further, is it not a fact that the increase in loans might cause land costs to go up? Is it not a fact also that the standard practice of the corporation is to make loans averaging about half the going price of the land for sale? These are two questions that concern me and which should be answered before clause 1 is passed.
I am still concerned about the proposition of a father borrowing for his son. This was the question I raised last night, and which the minister did not answer. Many other hon. members have referred to this matter of sons aged 16 and 17 years prepared to undertake farming after leaving school, and working with their fathers. I would like to see a father be able to borrow money for a son who is, say, 18 years of age. Earlier today, and not in connection with the Farm Credit Corporation, it was mentioned by an hon. member that 16 years of age was considered in Ontario to be an eligible age with respect to another matter. I wonder if age 16 also has a bearing with regard to a farmer borrowing money for his son in order that he may purchase land. Perhaps the minister would make a brief reply to the three questions I have dealt with particularly in my remarks, Mr. Chairman.

That appears to be the case, judging from the groans anyway. The first thing I am concerned about is something the minister mentioned last night. He said that in future any interest charged will take into account a provision for bad debts. This is to be found on page 4212 of Hansard, where the minister is reported as having said that interest would be charged, plus an amount for bad debts. In my view this is a wrong prin-20220-270
Farm Credit Act
ciple to be applied here. First of all, Mr. Chairman, why should any future borrower have to make up for any bad debt in respect of a loan that, perhaps on the advice of the Farm Credit Corporation adviser, somebody had obtained and for one reason or another was not able to repay? Why should anybody obtaining a loan from the corporation in the future have to make up for a bad debt which may have been incurred by the fault of the corporation.
If the department is going to take that attitude, I wonder how the corporation will react when an applicant comes in for a loan. Probably one of the first things they will think about is, "We want to make sure this is not going to be a bad debt". In other words, they will take the view that every loan they approve should be paid off 100 per cent. There may be many borderline applications where the people involved would end up being a good risk, but where the Farm Credit Corporation adviser at the time the loan was applied for may have felt it was not a good risk. The adviser may well have uppermost in his mind the thought that the corporation does not want to incur a bad debt, because if they did somebody in the future would have to make up for that bad debt and the corporation would be criticized for borrowers being obliged to pay a higher rate of interest to make up for it.
I see the minister shaking his head in disagreement, but I think this is what his words mean. I should like to quote from Hansard what the minister said with regard to this question:
We do not expect this will be much larger, and it will be plus an amount for bad debts.
To my mind this spells trouble. First of all the maximum use of the Farm Credit Corporation facilities will not be obtained because the corporation's adviser will be hesitant about approving a loan for fear it will result in a bad debt and somebody will question his decision. If this practice is followed, naturally any man who asks for a loan in the future will ask the question, "Why should I pay for somebody else's bad debt?" If there is a bad debt incurred by the corporation, I suggest this should be something the government should subsidize. I think the government should pay for these bad debts and should allow the Farm Credit Corporation adviser enough leeway so that he will not withhold a loan in respect of someone who might be a good risk.

Farm Credit Act
I hear voices on the other side of the chamber, Mr. Chairman. I do not know what the argument is over there because, as I said, this is the first piece of legislation the minister has introduced and the record of this government indicates that after scrutiny by the opposition they have had to change so many other things they have introduced. I think this is another of those areas with regard to which they should be prepared to accept some good suggestions. I ask the minister to reconsider his position on this matter and remove the provision that farmers taking out loans should pay for bad debts which may be incurred as a result of a decision made by the farm credit adviser, who may have been thinking properly and on the basis of information he had received but might not have made the right decision. If a bad debt is incurred I do not think it should be considered to be the fault of the Farm Credit Corporation adviser, and the government should revise its position in this regard and provide a subsidy if necessary to make up for any bad debts that are incurred. It should not be the responsibility of the borrowers to make up for bad debts. I wonder whether the minister would care to make any comment on this question, Mr. Chairman.

the additional $20,000. This would amount to a total annual payment over the whole amount of $40,000 of $2,834. The average interest rate on today's market would be 5f per cent and the average amortization over the whole period would be at 7.08 per cent. After 30 years the whole $40,000 loan would be retired. Perhaps I should explain at this time that when the person who had borrowed $40,000 was down to the last $15,000 he would still be paying 7.08 per cent principal and interest.
As I mentioned yesterday, the Farm Credit Act is a very close copy of similar acts in the United States and other countries, and is certainly an improvement over the old farm loan board; I do not think there is any doubt about that. The limits in the United States are $95,000; $65,000 for land and $30,000 for chattels.
These are some of the studies which we made during the last year and which I think fully justify the increase in the larger amounts. One group of grain farmers in Saskatchewan had an average capital investment of over $31,000. The average cash receipts for those farmers were $4,700 and the average net return was $1,400. Another group of farmers in the same area had an average investment of about $48,500. The cash receipts were $8,100 and the net returns were about $3,600. The net returns to the farmers with the larger capital investment were more than double those of the farmers with the smaller capital investment, and it is natural that they should be because there would probably be the same equipment, and that sort of thing, to take care of the larger economic unit. That is with regard to grain farmers.
Another example is that of the mixed grain and cattle farmers in Saskatchewan. Farms with a capital investment of $38,500 showed cash receipts of about $5,500 and a net return of about $1,400. Similar farms in the same area but with an average capital investment of $57,600 had cash receipts of $8,900 and net returns of $3,340.
The same relationship was shown on farms in Manitoba. There were three groups of grain farms. These had capital investments of about $37,000, $52,000 and $76,000. The cash incomes for this group amounted to about $10,000 with a $37,000 investment, $13,300 with a $52,000 investment and $21,300 with a $76,000 investment. The respective net returns by groups of farmers were about $5,200, $7,600 and $11,800.
A study of the livestock farms of Manitoba has shown that the same farmers with a capi-

tal investment of $13,500 had a net return of $1,700. As the amount of capital increased, the net return increased. Farmers with an investment of $55,000 showed an average net return of $6,400.
These are some of the methods by which we can attack these agricultural problems. I know that help is needed by a combination of methods. We need the assistance given by ARDA and some of these other measures, but I think the bill before us has a very important part to play in the setting up of economic units. This provision for making proper credit facilities available is closely tied in with our amendment concerning farm improvement loans, with the crop insurance bill now on the order paper and with the farm machinery bill which we hope to get on the order paper very shortly. I know this is not a complete answer; there must be proper markets, and so on. But we hope these amendments will bring about a marked improvement in the act for the benefit of farmers.
There is one other question I should like to answer. I believe it was raised last night by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who asked what the rates of interest were under Small Businesses Loans Act. I think we are completely consistent in making the proposals contained in this amendment. In this whole field of government lending, or government guarantee of loans, various practices are followed. Under the National Housing Act a rate of interest is prescribed in much the same way as it is proposed to do under this bill for loans in excess of $20,000 and $27,500.
Under the home improvement loans provisions, the banks make insured loans at a present interest rate of 6 per cent. The industrial development bank lends money to small industry at 7 per cent. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam yesterday referred to the Small Businesses Loans Act. These are bank loans, guaranteed by the government, and in this case the maximum interest authorized is 5 J per cent. The maximum amount of these loans is $25,000.
Then there are fisheries loans. These also are made through banks under government guarantee. The interest rate is 5 per cent and the maximum loan is $4,000. There has also been the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act under which loans have carried a 5 per cent interest rate to a maximum of $3,000. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, loans under which are made by banks under government guarantee, the interest rate is 5 per cent. The present maximum limit is $7,500. This brings us to the Farm

Credit Act and the present bill and, as the committee knows, the rate of interest on standard loans up to $20,000 and supervised loans up to $27,500 is not being disturbed.
So we think there is full justification for doing what is proposed here. It is consistent with practice in the past, and we think it is right, that after a certain minimum we can go on and charge the economic rate. This rate is based on what the government has to pay for money, plus the cost of administration and the reserve.

In the first place, Mr. Chairman, he must be a farmer. Probably I should explain subclause 1 of clause 3. Suppose a father has two sons who wish to take up farming. His own farm unit may not be large enough to support the two of them. He may wish to transfer to one of his sons but at the same time to assist the other son to buy a farm of his own. This son may have worked for years on the family farm and contributed labour at a relatively low cost to his father.
Although the father may wish to assist the son financially it may be that his own farm, while adequate for his needs, did not produce enough revenue that he could make savings and have the money available to assist his son. This clause would permit him to borrow from the corporation and turn the money over to his son to permit him to make a down payment on the purchase of another farm. The son, who would then have an equity in the farm he was buying, would be able to go to the corporation and obtain a loan under part III of the act, the part where there is supervision, to pay the balance of the purchase price of the farm and to purchase livestock and equipment.

I want to make now the remarks I originally intended to make on this amendment. First of all, I would like to remind the members of the committee that the subject of interest rates has been the core of the whole debate on farm credit ever since the bill was introduced originally. I should like to read into the record the original clause introduced in this house on June 29, 1959, and then I think the history will become dramatically clear. Section 9(c) read:
Interest rates on loans shall be at a rate that, in the opinion of the corporation, is sufficient to provide for the interest payable by the corporation to the Minister of Finance and the expenses of the corporation, including reasonable provision for reserves against losses.
This was the original draft brought into the house in June 1959. In those days we had on the government side a large number of members now sitting on the opposition side, who stood up in their places and said they did not want that provision as it was. The government of the day yielded to the mem-
Farm Credit Act
bers of the government party and changed that clause 16(c) to read as follows:
The interest rate on loans shall be 5 per cent per annum.
In the amendment proposed it is stated that section 16(c) shall be repealed, and that is why earlier today I mentioned the doubt in my mind whether the forces that want high interest rates back in Canada had won a victory over the Minister of Agriculture. I wonder, in view of the struggles we had in 1959 to get the principle of the stabilized interest rate of 5 per cent for agricultural loans, whether that principle has been lost to a degree in these new amendments, and particularly in this amending clause 4.
Once you get it accepted that you are going to depart one step from the principle of stabilized loans and apply a variable rate of interest to loans above a certain amount, it is not much of a step backwards to try and apply that principle-as finance people try to do-over the whole of the original part of the loan.
Today we have accepted in effect that we are going to put amendments through that will allow for the keeping of this 5 per cent principle on loans up to $20,000 under part II and on loans up to $27,500 under part III, but will the minister give the committee his assurance, and I hope with it the assurance of the whole government, that there will be no further steps taken to try and change the 5 per cent rate on the first part of the loans up to $20,000 and $27,500, to this variable amount?
This assurance from the minister would be a great help to us in the opposition. We belong to the group that fought for and won the principle of stabilized interest rates. Now the minister is varying the rate for the higher amounts. We are not going to quarrel with this too much, but if we do accept this one step does it mean the minister will be coming back and asking for the same principle to be applied to old loans?
The second question I would like to ask has to do with the variable part of loans. As I understand the principle now, when the interest rate goes up every three months, when the interest rate is set by the Department of Finance, the Farm Credit Corporation under this new amendment will be duty bound to sit down and decide what the interest rate is going to be for loans above $20,000 under part II and above $27,500 under part III. Will the new contracts needed for the next three months be at this new interest rate?

Farm Credit Act
If the answer to that question is yes, then my major question is this. What happens when interest rates turn down? Let us say the cost of money, plus the cost of running the corporation, totals 4J per cent-and this has happened-then will the additional amounts be at 4 i per cent, and the original amounts of $20,000 and $27,500 still be at 5 per cent? In other words will the interest rates follow steadily the fluctuating cost of money to the Farm Credit Corporation from the Department of Finance?
My third question, which is supplementary to the second one, is this. If a man has signed up today for a loan, part of which is going to be at 6| per cent, and next year the rate is down to 6 per cent, and down to 5 per cent two years from now, will he be given any opportunity to get a change in his contract or will he be stuck for the whole life of the contract at 6| per cent, even if the cost rate goes down?

This bringing in of principal payments is rather confusing, and the minister admitted that a little while ago. He says that for now the government is not going to change the 5 per cent rate, but I would like a little stronger assurance from the government than that, stating that the ordinary farmer will have guaranteed to him, for perpetuity actually, a stabilized interest rate. We have accepted the figure of 5 per 
cent, which I think has covered the history of borrowing for the last 30 or 40 years.
As a matter of fact, the government has lots of precedents in this regard. If you want to borrow money from the people, as is done under government annuities, you just go to the government office and they will tell you that for the period of your life annuity the maximum amount you can get is 4 per cent. They know this is the maximum they can guarantee, and the Canada pension plan talk is all based on 4 per cent. I point out to you that when you are asking people to lend their money to the government all you will give them on long term contract is 4 per cent. However, we, when we were the government, accepted this principle in reverse, and said that when lending money to farmers we would accept this long term average of 4 per cent, to which we added 1 per cent for costs. The minister has departed from this principle for loans above the previous limits. All I am asking for now is a little stronger assurance from the minister, representing the government, that the government has no intention now or in the foreseeable future-and when I say the foreseeable future, I mean as far ahead as 15, 20, 25 or 30 years-of changing this situation. A long term contract has been made with farmers of Canada that the interest rate will be stabilized, based on 4 per cent plus the cost of running the corporation, and if we could get this strong assurance from the minister-I know that some members of the government will fight with him, and the finance people will fight for the principle for which they have always fought-* I think we would be happy to go along with an interest rate which is a little higher on the higher rate of borrowing.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a question for the minister in relation to clause 4. However, at the outset I should like to inform him that I firmly believe it would be very desirable and much more acceptable if the government would arrive at a stabilized rate of interest with regard to loans in excess of $20,000 under part II and $27,500 under part III, instead of using the sliding scale of interest which they have put into these amendments. Last night the minister said, as I understood him, that in relation to loans in excess of $20,000 under part II and $27,500 under part III there would be an added amount to cover what it cost the government to borrow that money, plus the cost of operation of the corporation, plus an amount of, I believe he said no more than one quarter of 1 per cent in relation to bad debts. I am wondering what assurance the minister can give the house that this will not exceed one quarter of 1 per cent. I see nothing in the amendments as listed in Bill No. C-100 in regard to this and I am very interested in knowing just how the minister can assure the house that this will not exceed one quarter of 1 per cent.
Speaking on the desirability of maintaining a stabilized interest rate instead of having a sliding scale, I am thinking of the case which occurs quite frequently when a smaller farmer applies for a loan of possibly between $20,000 and $25,000; then when the consultants go out to look over the farm and make an assessment they sometimes, and in fact quite often, find that to make it an economic unit it is desirable for the applicant to request a larger loan. In such a case the man would be told, if he applied for $25,000 to make his unit economic, that he should ask for $30,000. However, on the first $20,000 he is going to be paying 5 per cent, but in regard to the larger amount recommended by the corporation the interest rate will go up quite excessively. I am thinking that we might find a farmer may not wish to pay these interest rates, and he will be put in quite a predicament as to

Farm Credit Act
whether to accept the recommendation of the consultant and apply for a loan of $30,000 or whether to leave it as originally applied for, in which case he would not be making it an economic unit in the eyes of the corporation. I think this is an area in which we could run into difficulty, and we should have a stabilized interest rate of possibly 5 per cent. I would like the minister to tell us what assurance he can give the committee that one quarter of 1 per cent will be the ultimate limit applied to the interest rate to cover bad debts.

Our experience in the past has been that it is less than one tenth of 1 per cent, and the loss has generally always occurred on the smaller loans. The hon. member suggests that quite often when a farmer is making application for a loan in order to make his unit economic it is suggested that he should ask for more money. In this regard I might say that all our branch managers were called in from all across Canada and were here for quite some time. We suggested to them that they should adopt a little more vigorous attitude in so far as loans were concerned, not to hold people down but to see that they did have an ample amount which would make their farms an economic unit. Sometimes the difference between 10 and 12 cows, in a cow and calf proposition, is the difference between $1,000 and $1,200 revenue; and the difference of another 100 acres would facilitate their paying back the loan much more easily, if they had enough money to provide for such an operation in the first instance. I have said all during the debate that this would not be more than one quarter of 1 per cent. It will more likely be below that-probably one eighth or something like that. This will be a reserve set up on that portion of the loan in excess of the $20,000 or the $27,500.
With regard to the stabilization of the interest rate, it is liable to slide up and down; but the farmer who borrows money will have a steady rate throughout the life of the loan. There will be no escalation clause in it. He knows that on the first $20,000 he will pay 5 per cent. If he were to borrow today he will pay 5| per cent plus the cost of the operation of the corporation, which is becoming smaller as time goes on due to the magnitude of the loans being made. The cost is about .87 of 1 per cent plus the one eighth of 1 per cent.

I should also like to make it quite clear that I was not criticizing the corporation in any way for suggesting in many cases a higher loan to make a farm a more economic unit. I think that is a very good feature of their assessments. I myself have had several cases where this has been done and it has worked out quite satisfactorily. I have also had cases where the loan was not approved to the amount the applicant wished. In these cases in the opinion of the farmer, of course, he felt he needed the amount to make the unit economic, whereas in many cases the corporation felt that his holdings did not justify a loan of that size. Here again we have a clash of opinions as to whether the amount of a loan would make the farm an economic unit. I did want to make it quite clear that I am not criticizing this aspect of the corporation, because I know they are very anxious to assess these farms to the best of their ability and to make a loan of the nature which will make a farm an economic unit.

Mr. Speaker, I am in agreement with the amendment, but I am concerned at the increased rate of interest which will be charged on the extra money. As the former minister of agriculture said, the members of our party put up a terrific fight both in front and behind the curtain with the Department of Finance to keep the interest rate at 5 per cent. Now it is going to be increased.
I think the Minister of Agriculture will agree that farming is a risky business. A farmer may have a crop failure and have to carry his payments over the year, and a high rate of interest could be very harmful. I am sure he would like a steady rate of 5 per cent right across the board, and I wonder whether the minister would be supported by his backbenchers and those interested in farming if they went to the Department of Finance and asked them to keep the interest rate down to 5 per cent. We have not heard from these backbenchers today, but we on this side should like to keep the rate of interest at 5 per cent. If the minister is interested in doing this, would he consider referring the matter back to the agriculture committee? I am sure he would get enough support from our members on the committee, and if the minister also felt that it should be 5 per cent on all of the loans he could bring the matter back to the house again.

this time. I can assure the hon. member that J feel that I do know farming, because I started out with nothing. I think all farmers will agree that this is not too much to ask, when you stop and think that last year, outside of the amount of money put up by the federal government, the farmers borrowed $235 million at interest rates in excess of 10 per cent. Therefore this act will help solve some of their problems. When you stop and think about it, an extra $5,000 on part II loans up to $25,000 costs only $75 a year amortized over 30 years.

Mr. Chairman, the minister seems to be very complacent today that the opening up of the interest rate in the second part of this proposal places the stabilized rate in the first part of this proposal in no danger. I cannot share the view he has expressed today. If he and the backbenchers across the way have been unable to hold the fort in this regard today, once this is in operation the demand to raise the rate on the first $20,000 will become much louder than it is at the present time, and it will only be a matter of time before the minister comes back to the house and says it has worked so well for those who have been paying the economic rate that all farmers should be paying the economic rate, and there will be very little criticism of that from them.
I think this legislation will be much better if there were a stabilized rate so that everyone would be treated alike, not only six months from now but a year or two years from now-or for whatever time a loan were taken out. I do not think it is too late at this time for the minister and the government to decide to do this. After all, the amount of money which might be involved for a year or two under the circumstances prevailing today is not so great when you compare it with the over-all needs of the agricultural industry and the entire budget of the nation. For that reason I ask not only the Minister of Agriculture but all members of the cabinet -and I am sorry to see so few of them here today-to take this whole problem into consideration.

speechtext:
In introducing this new aspect of the legislation the minister must have had some information either from within his department or from other sources respecting the need for loans of this type. He must have believed there were farmers who wished to borrow more than $20,000 or $27,500. I wonder if he has any information as to the number of loans the corporation anticipates making in this category in the first year. Farm credit advisers across the country must have suggested a possible figure. As the minister said, they met here in Ottawa and it was on the basis of suggestions made by them and by others that these amendments were brought forward. Could the minister indi-

cate, for example, how many loans of this order were requested in the course of last year.
I am asking this question for the following reason: I am wondering how much money we can possibly expect to save by increasing interest rates above 5 per cent. If only a few loans are to be taken out, it seems to me we should drop this whole clause entirely. I feel that by adopting it we would be opening the door to a revision of the act in a year or two upon the recommendation of the minister's supporters, or some financial firms, to the effect that this is not the right way in which to conduct business, with the result that the rate would be increased from 5 per cent to whatever rate might be necessary to recoup expenses, write off debts and so on. The minister said he anticipates that a certain amount of money will not be recovered under the 5 per cent provision. If this is the case, I wonder how much he will save by increasing the interest rate above 5 per cent; I am wondering whether it is worth the trouble.

speechtext: About 13 per cent of the loans last year were for the maximum amount. We anticipate that these people will be back, because to most of this 13 per cent the amount available was not sufficient. Of course, the percentage will grow as time goes on, as more people become familiar with these terms of the legislation. I think a great many people in Canada are still not familiar with this act. I believe there is still a great educational program to be carried out. The need for these additional amounts is substantial and the number of applications will surprise hon. members. subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Since the minister has indicated that perhaps 13 per cent took the maximum loans last year, it is conceivable that 13 per cent more will take them out in the coming year. If we have provided loans to the extent of $100 million, we can expect another $10 million or $12 million in the following year. Therefore what we are really concerned about here is not an interest rate of 5 per cent on that $12 million, but on just a fraction of it. So it is obvious that the government will really save very little by introducing this legislation. I repeat that the amount of saving to the government is going to be infinitesimal, but to the individual farmer the amount is going to be considerable as he pays off his loan over a period of years.
If we must concern ourselves about trying to remedy the financial situation of the gov-

ernment, then let the minister say so. Are we going to provide legislation that will be beneficial to the farmer, even at the expense of a little money from the government? This is the important feature. As I have already pointed out, I am concerned that we are opening the door for the future in such a way that the interest rate will be increased still more.
We still do not know what the rate is going to be. The minister has not indicated whether it is going to be 6 or 7 per cent. But if the minister wants to raise the rate in the future and wishes to amend the legislation again for that purpose, he will be able to say, on the basis of the precedent we are setting here, that the corporation is again losing money and the rate should be raised.
Is the minister prepared to accept the responsibility of saying that money must be saved for the government, or is he introducing this legislation for the benefit of the farmers? Since the minister cannot give us an indication of the rate we must assume that the amount of money the government is going to save will be very small and that in effect the government is not concerned about the welfare of the borrowers but is perhaps trying to assist the Minister of Finance. What position is the government taking? Whom are they helping?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Our whole purpose, of course, is to help the farmers. Under this amendment we are doubling the size of loans. I can see the Farm Credit Corporation lending a total of $1 billion in the future. I do not know how high it is going to go but at that time I suppose it will be a revolving sort of thing. Many of these loans will never be completely repaid by the original borrower. There is provision in the bill that when a farmer passes on or retires his son can pick up the loan and carry on in much the same way as a man who owns a house and dies before the mortgage is completely paid off. He may own the house all his life and never get it completely paid off.
This is a long range policy. It is tied in with three other pieces of legislation that we hope to have before the house in the next 30 days. It is difficult to explain some of these things until we have all parts of the picture together. This particular piece of legislation will do twice as much, so far as providing capital for farmers is concerned. At the time the Farm Credit Corporation was established I think it was possibly adequate then. But times have changed and now we need to take
Farm. Credit Act
the next step, which we have done. We are certainly not discriminating against small farmers because we have not changed the situation so far as they are concerned. But in the case of the farmer who wishes to borrow above a certain amount we are simply trying to see that he does not have to pay an excessive amount of interest, that he does not have to go outside of the Farm Credit Corporation and obtain money at 12 or 15 per cent. I think this provision takes care of this situation.

I think the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose had a good idea when he suggested that this matter should be referred to the committee on agriculture for consideration at one meeting at least. Possibily that would give government members an opportunity to support this provision. party support his stand, although he did get up in his place a few moments ago and put forward that view.
